summary:
GO/NO-GO is an interactive space mission design game that transforms aerospace engineering into an accessible, hands-on learning experience. Players become mission engineers, design spacecraft, select instruments and launch vehicles, manage limited resources, and make critical decisions throughout a simulated mission.

Inspired by real NASA mission development processes, the game features four missions: Semeru Watch, Archipelago Link, Lunar Ice Hunter, and Solar Sentinel. Players experience realistic engineering trade-offs, interactive 3D orbital simulations, unexpected mission anomalies, and collaborative GO/NO-GO launch decisions.

By integrating authentic NASA Earth, Moon, and solar imagery with simplified scientific models, GO/NO-GO connects theoretical knowledge with practical problem-solving.

Our goal is to make space science and engineering accessible to students worldwide, especially those with limited access to STEM resources. With bilingual support, offline accessibility, and multiplayer collaboration, GO/NO-GO empowers the next generation of space explorers to learn through experimentation, teamwork, and meaningful failure.
details:
GO/NO-GO — Every Decision Shapes the Mission

The Problem

Space mission engineering is often taught through isolated concepts, making it difficult for students to understand how scientific objectives, spacecraft design, resource limitations, and operational decisions influence one another.

GO/NO-GO bridges this gap by transforming the complete mission development lifecycle into an interactive educational experience.

Our Solution

GO/NO-GO is a browser-based space mission simulation game where players take responsibility for designing, launching, and operating spacecraft. It supports individual and collaborative gameplay for up to four players.

The experience is organized into five stages:

  1. Mission Briefing: Select a mission, establish priorities, and identify measurable requirements.
  2. Spacecraft Design: Configure instruments, propulsion, power systems, communication equipment, spacecraft platforms, orbits, and launch vehicles.
  3. GO/NO-GO Review: Evaluate mission readiness through four engineering stations and resolve conflicting technical requirements.
  4. Mission Simulation: Launch the spacecraft, visualize orbital operations in 3D, and respond to unexpected events.
  5. Post-Mission Analysis: Evaluate performance, understand engineering failures, compare the design with real space missions, and improve the spacecraft.

Four Missions, Real-World Challenges

  • Semeru Watch: Design an Earth observation mission to monitor volcanic activity in Indonesia.
  • Archipelago Link: Develop a satellite communication mission to support remote island communities.
  • Lunar Ice Hunter: Design a lunar exploration mission to investigate hydrogen and potential water ice near the lunar poles.
  • Solar Sentinel: Develop a solar observation mission to study solar activity and space weather.

Creativity and Innovation

Our central innovation is the GO/NO-GO decision-making system. Instead of simply rewarding players for selecting the most advanced technology, the game requires them to balance competing engineering objectives.

Every design decision affects interconnected resources, including mass, power, budget, communication capacity, data, mission lifetime, and propulsion.

In multiplayer mode, players control separate engineering stations, encouraging communication, negotiation, and collective responsibility before launch.

The game includes:

  • Four missions with nine mission priorities.
  • 62 configurable options across 11 categories.
  • Seven orbital configurations and five launch vehicles.
  • Twelve possible mission events.
  • Three difficulty levels.
  • A mission scoring system with a maximum of 1,000 points.
  • An educational Codex covering 29 concepts.
  • Comparisons with 17 real-world space missions.

Scientific Foundation and NASA Data

GO/NO-GO integrates authentic NASA resources directly into its educational experience.

NASA Blue Marble imagery provides the Earth visualization, while Aqua MODIS and VIIRS Black Marble imagery support the Indonesian missions. Solar Sentinel incorporates Solar Dynamics Observatory imagery, and Lunar Ice Hunter uses lunar textures derived from Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter data.

The simulation incorporates simplified scientific relationships, including Kepler's third law, the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, orbital geometry, solar array sizing, battery consumption, and orbital revisit calculations.

NASA mission development resources also informed the engineering stations and mission review process.

These models are intentionally simplified for educational gameplay rather than professional spacecraft engineering.

Technology and Development

The application was developed using:

  • HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript ES modules.
  • Three.js for interactive 3D spacecraft and orbital visualization.
  • MQTT over WebSocket for multiplayer communication.
  • HiveMQ and EMQX public MQTT brokers.
  • Service Workers for offline accessibility.
  • Python for local development.
  • Node.js for automated testing.
  • GitHub for version control.
  • Vercel for public deployment.

Our repository documents 31 automated tests covering mission calculations, flight simulation, scoring, multilingual functionality, and multiplayer rules.

Intended Impact

Our goal is to make aerospace engineering understandable and accessible regardless of a learner's technical background or geographical location.

GO/NO-GO is free to access, requires no installation or account, supports English and Bahasa Indonesia, and enables offline gameplay after the initial visit.

By connecting space science with practical Indonesian challenges, such as volcanic monitoring and communication across remote islands, we aim to demonstrate how space technology can address problems on Earth.

We envision GO/NO-GO becoming an educational resource for STEM classrooms, science communities, and future space enthusiasts worldwide.

Responsible Development

GO/NO-GO originated from our team's genuine curiosity about rocket launches and space mission simulations. The original concept and educational objectives were independently conceived by our team without AI assistance.

We used Claude by Anthropic to assist with implementation, text generation, translation, testing, and debugging. All final design and development decisions remained under our team's responsibility.

AI-assisted development is disclosed in our project documentation. The game uses authentic NASA imagery rather than AI-generated images.

Future Development

We plan to expand the experience with dedicated classroom tools, additional mission scenarios, unrestricted engineering sandbox modes, and competitive multiplayer challenges.
